items.title: Start With GoWebComponents
items.blurb: Module install, public package surface, and the first ui.Render path.

sections.heading: What GoWebComponents is
paragraphs: GoWebComponents is a Go plus WebAssembly UI framework with a React-style component model, hooks, typed HTML builders, routing, shared state, SSR, hydration, and devtools.
This concept page is the lightweight on-ramp: explain why the public surface is split into ui, html, state, fetch, router, and companion tooling before readers drop into raw API tables.

sections.heading: First render path
paragraphs: Start with module install, a js/wasm build target, and a minimal ui.Render call that mounts into #app. That gets readers to the first successful browser render fast.
Keep the first concept page practical: package imports, the build target, and a tiny component tree are enough to make the rest of the docs site feel grounded.

content.callout: A good GoWebComponents concept page should explain how the Go, js/wasm, and package-level authoring model fit together before the reader opens a single reference table.

items.title: ui.CreateElement and Components
items.blurb: Typed component construction and the basic unit of composition in GoWebComponents.

content.summary: Builds a typed component node from a Go function component and props struct so the runtime can render and diff it like any other node in the tree.

params.name: component
params.description: Go function component that renders a node tree for the provided props.

params.name: props
params.description: Typed props payload passed into the component function.

notes: Keep component APIs tied to real package names and real return types so readers can copy examples directly into Go code.
This is the core composition primitive beneath the friendlier example pages and larger routed app shells.

items.title: ui.UseState and Local State
items.blurb: Local state, shared atoms, and the mutation rules that keep GoWebComponents predictable.

content.summary: Creates local component state with Get, Set, and Update helpers. Use it for view-local behavior; move to the state package when multiple readers need the same source of truth.

params.name: initial
params.description: Initial state value for the current component instance.

content.example:
count := ui.UseState(0)
count.Update(func(previous int) int { return previous + 1 })
notes: Prefer Update when the next value depends on the previous committed value.
Use ui.UseState for local behavior and state.UseAtom or state.UseDerived when the value should outlive one component subtree.

items.title: SSR Walkthrough
items.blurb: How server rendering, hydration, and data boundaries fit together.

sections.heading: Rendering model
paragraphs: GoWebComponents SSR docs should explain the real sequence clearly: render HTML with ui.RenderToString, emit bootstrap payloads, ship markup, then resume with hydration on the client.
Keep diagrams optional, but the prose should still stand on its own for engineers trying to understand route data reuse, bootstrap ownership, and when hydration is worth the complexity.

sections.heading: Why this belongs in Concepts
paragraphs: This is not a bare function reference. Readers need the route-aware mental model first: what runs on the server, what resumes in wasm, and where bootstrap payloads and loaders belong.

content.callout: GoWebComponents SSR guidance should explain how server HTML, bootstrap payloads, and client hydration cooperate before the API reference drills into exact helper signatures.
content.code:
ui.RenderToString(app)
  -> ui.RenderBootstrapScript(...)
  -> send HTML
  -> load wasm bundle
  -> ui.Hydrate(...)
  -> router.HydrateMount(...)

items.title: fetch.UseResource Data Flow
items.blurb: Typed resource loading, pending states, and cache-aware refetch rules.

content.summary: Loads typed async data for the current view, exposes loading and error state, and gives the page an explicit reload hook without inventing a separate query language.

params.name: loader
params.description: Typed loader function that returns the resource value or an error.

notes: Expose loading, ready, and error behavior clearly in the docs so readers can tell when UseResource is enough and when they need cached resources.
Link this page to the fetch and SSR bootstrap examples so the async story stays coherent across the docs site.

items.title: Typed HTML and Design Language
items.blurb: How typed html builders, semantic markup, and the docs-site design language fit together.

sections.heading: Typed markup first
paragraphs: GoWebComponents design docs should start with typed html builders and semantic structure before they talk about decorative styling. The framework earns its keep by making real DOM shape explicit in Go code.
Once the markup model is clear, document the site-level design language: gradients, spacing, contrast, and how example pages stay recognizably part of one product surface.

sections.heading: Docs implication
paragraphs: Because concepts are markdown-like, they are perfect for showing rationale, constraints, and migration guidance rather than raw API surface area.

content.callout: For GoWebComponents, design-system guidance should connect typed markup, semantic structure, and example-shell branding instead of pretending visual language is separate from the component model.

items.title: Build and Dev Workflow
items.blurb: The minimal commands for building wasm, serving examples, and iterating on GoWebComponents apps.

content.signature: go build, tools/dev.ps1, npm --prefix ../tools/devtools run dev:examples
content.summary: The practical workflow surface for this repo: build wasm with Go, use the example server for catalog browsing, and use the hot reload helpers when iterating on a single app.

params.name: command
params.description: One of dev, build, preview, export, or deploy.

content.returns: built wasm, local dev server, or static site output depending on the command
notes: Keep workflow docs tied to the actual repository commands instead of inventing a generic CLI that does not exist.
This page should connect directly to examples, testing, and GitHub Pages deployment guidance.

items.title: Companion Packages and Plugins
items.blurb: How companion packages and the experimental plugin surface extend GoWebComponents without reaching into internals.

sections.heading: Extension boundaries
paragraphs: GoWebComponents should prefer companion packages built on public APIs first. The plugin surface exists for explicit application-owned extension points, not as a backdoor into framework internals.
These pages work best as prose-first docs that explain capability checks, host ownership, and stability tiers before they dump hook signatures.

sections.heading: Authoring guidance
paragraphs: Explain lifecycle order, capabilities, and versioning strategy in human language first. Then link to the actual plugin and ecosystem docs for the exact interfaces and support policy.

content.callout: GoWebComponents extension guidance should make one thing obvious: stay on documented public APIs unless the companion or plugin surface explicitly promises more.
